name: Death Valley National Park
tagline: Salt flats, golden badlands and wind-shaped dunes below desert mountains.

photo.alt: Golden sand dunes, with heavy shadows and wave patterns in the foreground and bare mountains in the background
photo.caption: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes

intro: Death Valley holds the lowest point in North America, a white salt flat lying beneath mountains that climb more than two miles above it. Golden badlands, rippled sand dunes and ridgetop overlooks make it a place of wide silence and changing light. Scattering ashes is not allowed anywhere in the park, out of respect for the Timbisha Shoshone Tribe, but it remains a remarkable place to gather and remember together.

scatterSummary: Scattering ashes from human cremation is prohibited throughout Death Valley National Park.
scatterFacts: Superintendent's Compendium (approved November 19, 2025), 36 CFR 2.62(b): scattering ashes from human cremation is prohibited.
The park explains that Death Valley is a culturally sensitive area and that the prohibition respects the wishes of the Timbisha Shoshone Tribe.
No permit is available for scattering in the park.

planNote.heading: A Farewell Without Scattering
planNote.text: Ash scattering is not allowed anywhere in Death Valley National Park. The park prohibits it to respect the wishes of the Timbisha Shoshone Tribe. If you plan to bring your loved one's cremated remains for a visit, keep them in a secure, non-breakable container, confirm your plans with the park first, and take the remains with you when you leave. Arrange any scattering separately at a location where it is legally permitted.

beforeYouGo: The park is open year-round, 24 hours a day. Paved entrances: CA 190 from Death Valley Junction, SR 374 from Beatty, Nevada, and CA 178 from Shoshone on the east side; CA 190 from Olancha (SR 136 from Lone Pine) and SR 178 from Trona on the west side. There is no public transportation and no cell service along most park roads. Hiking is not advised after 10 am in summer; carry plenty of water in every season. Check the park's road conditions page, since floods close roads.

destinations.name: Badwater Basin

photo.alt: A large pool of water with mountains reflected in the background and a darkening sky

destinations.description: Walk down the boardwalk and out onto a floor of white salt, 282 feet below sea level, the lowest ground in North America. Look up at the cliffs of the Black Mountains and you can spot a sign marking sea level high above your heads. Across the valley, Telescope Peak rises more than two miles over the place you are standing. Walk a little farther together and the salt breaks into geometric polygons, a quiet, otherworldly setting for remembering someone who loved wide-open places.

plan.distance: 1 mi round trip to the edge of the salt flat
plan.accessibility: ADA accessible ramp to a wooden boardwalk; the surface beyond is firm and wide (NPS)
plan.bestTime: Hiking not advised after 10 am in summer
plan.scattering: Prohibited throughout the park. See below.

drive.route: From Furnace Creek, drive south on Badwater Road about 17 miles (30 minutes) to the paved parking lot.

trail.name: Badwater Salt Flat
steps: Follow the ramp down to the wooden boardwalk beside the spring-fed pool.
Continue out onto the salt flat; the best salt polygons are on a 1.5 to 2 mile round-trip walk.
notes: Do not attempt the walk when it is hot. Boating and flotation devices are prohibited on the seasonal lake.

destinations.name: Zabriskie Point

photo.alt: Striped yellow and brown hills of bare stone, with sunlight beginning to hit distant mountains and a mostly cloudy sky

destinations.description: From this rise, yellow and brown badlands fold away below you, carved into ridges and gullies by water that rarely falls. Manly Beacon juts up in the middle of it all, and beyond it the salt flats and the Panamint Mountains fill the horizon. Sunrise and sunset paint the hills in shifting color, so come early or stay late and watch it together. The more adventurous can wander down into the badlands while others keep the view.

plan.distance: 0.25 mi paved walk uphill from parking; Badlands Loop 2.7 mi loop
plan.difficulty: Easy to the viewpoint; Moderate on the Badlands Loop
plan.accessibility: Listed as wheelchair accessible (NPS); the paved path climbs a hill
plan.scattering: Prohibited throughout the park. See below.

drive.route: Drive east on Highway 190 from the Furnace Creek Visitor Center, about 15 minutes, to the Zabriskie Point parking area.

trail.name: Zabriskie Point path and Badlands Loop
steps: Walk the paved path up the hill to the viewpoint.
For more, pick up the Badlands Loop at the parking lot and watch for the small signs at each major intersection.

destinations.name: Dantes View

photo.alt: Looking from Dante's View across the Badwater Basin salt pan to Telescope Peak, 11,049 feet, at the top of the Panamint Mountains

destinations.description: High on the crest of the Black Mountains, 5,575 feet above Badwater Basin, the whole valley lies open beneath you: swirling white salt flats, and the Panamint Range on the far side. A local man once told a governor this was the one view that made him stop and look. Walk a little way north along the ridge to find a quieter spot, and if you stay after dark, the stars of this Dark Sky Park come out overhead.

plan.distance: Roadside overlook; distance from parking not published
plan.bestTime: Sunrise, sunset, or after dark for stars
plan.scattering: Prohibited throughout the park. See below.

drive.route: Leave Highway 190 for Dantes View Road and follow it to its end, about a 45-minute drive from Furnace Creek.

destinations.name: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes

photo.alt: The best time of day to visit dunes are early morning, late afternoon and under a full moon

destinations.description: There is no trail here, only sand, ripples and the long shadows of morning and evening. Mesquite trees twist up through the dunes, and in spring their branches fill with green leaves and yellow flowers. Choose your own way toward the tallest dune, stopping whenever someone wants to sit and look back at the mountains. After sunset the dunes become one of the park's darkest places for watching the stars come out together.

plan.distance: 2 mi round trip to the tallest dune
plan.accessibility: No official trail; walking on loose sand
plan.bestTime: Sunrise or sunset; hiking not advised after 10 am in summer
plan.scattering: Prohibited throughout the park. See below.

drive.route: Highway 190 to the paved dunes parking lot just east of Stovepipe Wells Village, about 30 minutes west of Furnace Creek.

trail.name: Cross-country walk to the tallest dune
steps: From the parking lot, choose your own route across the dunes; the summit of the high dune is about 1 mile each way.
notes: Watch your step and do not disturb animal burrows. Pets are not allowed on the dunes.

destinations.name: Golden Canyon to Red Cathedral
destinations.description: Step into Golden Canyon and its walls rise around you in shades of yellow, with ripples left by ancient water preserved in the stone. The path climbs gently up the canyon floor, past colorful side canyons and the remains of an old road taken by a flash flood. At the end waits Red Cathedral, a natural amphitheater of tall, fluted red walls. It is a walk for talking along the way and for falling quiet when you arrive.

plan.distance: 3 mi round trip to Red Cathedral
plan.accessibility: Rocky canyon route with minor scrambling over ledges about 4 ft high and under low overhangs
plan.bestTime: Hiking not advised after 10 am in summer
plan.scattering: Prohibited throughout the park. See below.

drive.route: From Highway 190, drive 2 miles south on Badwater Road to the paved Golden Canyon Trailhead lot.

trail.name: Golden Canyon Trail to Red Cathedral
steps: Walk gradually uphill through the rocky corridor of Golden Canyon.
Most hikers turn around at the Red Cathedral junction; continue another 0.5 mi for Red Cathedral.
Return the same way, or follow signs toward Zabriskie Point and Gower Gulch for the 7.8 mi circuit (Strenuous).
notes: Take the official map with you. No restroom along the trail.
